The situation

Every system running, and the meter running faster

See the detail

Your resort has three guest towers with 3,000 rooms, and occupancy runs about 85%. Each tower has its own water meter. Water and sewer both come from the city, and sewer is billed on the water meter, so water that goes down a drain is paid for twice.

The central plant has four large chillers, each with its own cooling tower cell. Three secondary pumps push the chilled water around the property. Condensing boilers make hot water for guest rooms, the laundry and the pools.

The rest of the water use is the in-house laundry with two tunnel washers, three heated pools, and 8.5 hectares of landscape on its own water service. The casino, convention centre and kitchens complete the site. Your climate is hot and dry with summer storms, so weather matters for the landscape and the cooling towers.

Most large hotels are in this position. The building management system keeps every space comfortable and every pump running, and each system is individually reasonable. What it does not do is notice that one tower draws more at 3 a.m. than its guests could, or that one cooling cell drains twice what its twin does. In a hotel every cubic metre is paid for twice, once as water and once as sewer, which is why the meters are where most of this money sits.

The approach

Find the loss, find the cause, price it, confirm it

See the detail

AquaMesh does not assume a fixed percentage. It starts from the plant's existing control-system and historian data and works through five steps.

01Detect

169 measuring points were read from the plant's own records. Every unit was compared with its identical twin, day by day, across 150 days, and every flow and power figure was held up against a balance.

02Diagnose

Each symptom was tested against what the instrument measures and how it typically misleads, to separate process problems from instrument problems. They resolved into 8 causes and 1 reading that needs a field check.

03Price

Each cause was priced from measured quantities, the plant's own curves and its own unit costs, against its own best comparable unit, never a design figure.

04Route a response

Each cause became one specific action with an owner and a timing. AquaMesh recommends; operators decide. Nothing is actuated.

05Verify

Each cause carries a metric and a target, tracked against a baseline from this same record, normalised for load and weather.

CAUSE 1

Tower 2 draws 2.1 m³/h through the night that its peers do not

$102,927/yrmeasured

Between 2:00 and 4:00 almost nobody uses water, so what a building draws then is mostly what leaks. Tower 2 draws 5.7 litres an hour per occupied room at that time; the other towers draw 3.3. That is 2.1 m³/h running all night, and it does not stop in the morning: across the whole day tower 2 uses about 2.4 m³/h more than its occupancy explains. Running toilets, fill valves and a stuck pressure-reducing bypass are the usual places it goes, and every cubic metre is billed twice, once as water and once as sewer.

What the data shows

Water nobody is using
2.14 m³/h
51 m³ a day
Daytime excess
2.4 m³/h
whole-day use above what occupancy explains: the leak runs all day

What it means

Water that runs through the night and carries on through the day points to a leak or a stuck valve somewhere in the tower, not to guest use. The data cannot say where, so a room-by-room and riser check is the way to find it. Left alone, it keeps running every hour of every day and is billed twice.

What the operator does

Walk tower 2 floor by floor at night with the riser valves: dye-test toilets, check fill valves and the pressure-reducing station bypass. Repeat the night reading after each floor to see the flow fall.

How it is confirmed

Tower 2 night flow per occupied room. Target: about 3.3 L/h, the other towers' level.

CAUSE 2

Washer 2 uses 1.9× the water per kilogram of linen of its twin

$80,507/yrmeasured

Washer 2 and Washer 1 wash the same linen. Washer 1 uses 6.2 litres per kilogram; washer 2 has gone from 9.7 to 11.5. A tunnel washer reuses its rinse water for the next load's wash; when the reuse tank's valve is stuck to drain, every load takes fresh water, and 45% of it then has to be heated to 54 °C.

Repair washer 2's reuse-tank valve and restore rinse-water reuse; check the wash recipe against washer 1's.

CAUSE 4

The chilled water pumps run flat out against their own valves

$58,735/yrmeasured

The chilled water pumps run at full speed and hold the header pressure by choking their discharge valves, which sit at about 62% open and take 91 kPa out of the water. Measured at the pump terminals the pumps turn 69% of their electricity into pressure and flow; 25% of the power is then burnt across the valves. A variable-speed drive or a trimmed impeller gives the same header pressure without it.

What the data shows

Valve position
62 % open
duty pumps, daily average
Pressure across the valves
91 kPa
a control valve needs about 30 kPa
Pump electrical to hydraulic
69 %
at the terminals
Power burnt across valves
84 kW
56 kW above the minimum

What it means

The pumps make more pressure than the system needs, and the valves then throw the extra away as heat. You pay for that electricity every hour the pumps run. A variable-speed drive or a trimmed impeller would deliver the same header pressure without wasting it.

What the operator does

Fit variable-speed drives on the duty chilled water pumps (or trim impellers) and control header pressure on speed, leaving the valves near fully open.

How it is confirmed

Chilled water pumps: kWh per cubic metre delivered. Target: about 0.120 kWh/m³ at the same header pressure.

What it means

Each backwash on Pool 2 is the same size as on the other pools, so the cause is that it backwashes far more often. Its filter pressure also stays low, which suggests it is being cleaned early, on a timer or a trigger set too low. Fixing the trigger should cut both the backwash water and the fresh water added to replace it.

What the operator does

Put pool 2's backwash on filter pressure, like the others, instead of the timer.

CAUSE 6

Chiller 2 uses 7% more power per ton than its twins

$49,507/yrmeasured

Chiller 2 makes the same chilled water as the chillers beside it, on the same condenser water. It started the record level with them and now uses 7% more electricity per ton of cooling. Its condenser approach, the gap between the refrigerant and the water leaving the condenser, has opened from 1.2 to 3.6 °C while its twins hold 0.9. That is the signature of fouled condenser tubes: scale or biofilm insulating them from the cooling water.

What the data shows

Power per ton against its twins
98 → 105 %
ratio, start to end, days both ran
Condenser approach
1.2 → 3.6 °C
twins 0.9 °C
Extra power
47 kW
at the end of the record

What it means

Chiller 2 started the record level with its twins and has slowly worsened, which points to fouling building up in the condenser tubes and not to a sudden fault. The data cannot confirm the cause, so a tube inspection is the next step. If it is left alone it will likely keep getting worse, and you will pay more power for every ton of cooling it makes.

What the operator does

Brush chiller 2's condenser tubes at the next low-load window and have the water-treatment vendor check the scale and biofilm programme on its tower.

How it is confirmed

Chiller 2 kW per ton and condenser approach. Target: kW per ton level with its twins, approach back near 0.9 °C.

CAUSE 7

The landscape is watered on a fixed schedule, rain or not

$41,166/yrestimated

The irrigation runs the same depth every night, 796 m³ a night on average, whatever the weather did that day. The plants' need moves with evaporation, which the site's own weather station logs, and with rain. Across the record the landscape needed about 103,563 m³ and got 118,555; on 7 of the 7 rainy days it was watered as if it had not rained. A weather-based controller waters to the day's evaporation and skips after rain.

What the data shows

Water applied
118,555 m³
149 nights in the record

103,563 m³
evaporation × crop factor 0.75 ÷ 75% efficiency, less 80% of rain
Watered after rain
7 of 7 days
rain over 3 mm
Excess this season
15,833 m³
only nights above need are counted

What it means

The schedule does not respond to weather, so the landscape gets the same water on a cool, wet day as on a hot, dry one. Watering after rain is the clearest waste, because the plants had no need of it. A controller that follows your weather station would cut the excess without leaving the landscape short.

What the operator does

Switch the irrigation controller to evaporation-based scheduling from the site's weather station, with a rain skip, and audit the zone run-times against plant type.

How it is confirmed

Irrigation volume against evaporation-based need. Target: within 10% of need, zero after rain.

CAUSE 8

Cooling tower B's controlling conductivity probe has slid out of calibration, so the tower drains water it should keep

$18,850/yrmeasured

Cooling tower B has two conductivity probes on the same water. They agreed at the start of the record and have since moved 18% apart. Independently, the water balance (water in, water drained, water evaporated) and the incoming water's conductivity both say the second probe is right. The first is reading about 19% off, and it is the one the tower's own reuse calculation and drain control follow, so the plant displays 5.5× reuse while the tower really reuses its water 4.6 times. The tower drains extra water to hold a number that is not real.

−0.0 %

Probe A against the balance
+18.8 %

What it means

The tower is being controlled by a reading that is wrong, and the plant screen hides it by showing the target was met. The water balance and the incoming water both back the second probe, so the first probe is the one to recalibrate or replace. Until then the tower keeps draining more than it needs to, and nobody sees it on the display.

What the operator does

Calibrate or replace the controlling probe on cooling tower B against a bench conductivity reading, and have the drain controller read the average of the two probes.

How it is confirmed

Cooling tower B: probe agreement and measured reuse. Target: probes within 2%, measured reuse back to 5.5×.

One finding is not counted

They are shown because they are worth acting on this week. A meter error is money only once you know which meter is wrong; a safety finding has no price, and should not need one.

SAFETY

Tower 3's hot water comes back at 46.5 °C, below the 51 °C water-safety plans rely on

$0measurednot counted in the total

Hot water leaves the plant at 60.5 °C and should come back from the far end of each riser no cooler than about 51 °C (124 °F). That margin is what keeps Legionella from growing in the pipework. Tower 3's return has averaged 46.5 °C over the last quarter and was below 51 °C on 100% of days; the other towers return at 54.7 °C. It costs nothing on the bill. It is a guest-safety and liability exposure, and the fix is usually a balancing valve.

What the data shows

Tower 3 return
46.5 °C
last quarter
Return guidance
51 °C
124 °F, common water-safety practice
Other towers
54.7 °C
same plant, same supply

What it means

This one is not about savings. Water that stays this far below the safe return temperature gives Legionella room to grow in the pipework, and the reading has been steady and never reaches the guidance. Because the other towers on the same plant and supply return warmer, the problem looks specific to tower 3's piping. Treat it as the first job to fix, and have the water-safety plan owner confirm the right response.

What the operator does

Check and rebalance tower 3's recirculation balancing valves, confirm with a calibrated thermometer at the farthest riser, and record it in the water management programme.

How it is confirmed

Tower 3 hot-water return temperature. Target: at or above 51 °C at every riser.

What AquaSpectra does and does not claim. AquaSpectra's BOD reading is calibrated to your own lab results. Is it right?

The audit was checked against the plant's own truth

See the detail

This plant is a physical simulation, built so the answer is known. Eight faults were built into it. The audit read only the historian export, the way it would read yours, and priced what it found. The simulator was then re-run with each fault removed, on the same weather and the same load, and the difference priced at the same unit costs. The audit never saw that.
